newsitem.title: USA: U.S. assessing need for troops in Zaire.
newsitem.headline: U.S. assessing need for troops in Zaire.

text.p: The United States will decide in the next few days if it needs to send troops to Zaire as it weighs the outcome of the mass movement of refugees home to Rwanda, administration officials said on Sunday.

"We have not made a decision on that yet," Defence Secretary William Perry said on NBC Television's "Meet the Press" programme. "We have made a decision to do the planning and pre-positioning. We have about 2,000 people and airplanes ready to provide logistics..."
Perry said the final decision on sending troops would be made shortly. "Certainly in the next few days," he said.

But he appeared less firmly fixed on the need for U.S. troops than appeared to be the case last week before the stream of tens of thousands of refugees began heading home to Rwanda, saying at one point "we are not the Salvation Army."
No decision is expected until midweek, according to administration officials.

Madeleine Albright, U.S. ambassador to the United Nations, said high-level representatives of countries planning to send troops to help in the relief efforts in Zaire would meet at the U.S. European military headquarters in Stuttgart in Germany on Tuesday and Wednesday.

She said on CNN's "Late Edition With Frank Sesno" that between 300,000 and 400,000 refugees had crossed into Rwanda and the flow continued at 12,000 to 15,000 an hour. "There are 300,000 waiting to go," she said, but added that "there are still a lot of missing people" who may be elsewhere in Zaire.

Administration officials said the U.S. delegation to Stuttgart would be made up of "very high level officials" from State, Defence and other departments involved, but the makeup of the delegation had not yet been decided.
On Saturday, President Bill Clinton spoke by telephone with South African President Nelson Mandela for about 15 minutes to press for regional participation in the mission.
A team of 40 U.S. military planners is in Zaire doing advance work on any U.S. deployment of troops, who Perry said would be mostly logistical personnel.
Perry told a news conference on Saturday that "It is possible that our plan, the allied plan ... will be modified" as a result of the movement of refugees.
"We are standing by in a ready mode to move forward with humanitarian support," he said.
Clinton last week agreed to send up to 5,000 troops to the region to join in a humanitarian relief effort to help up to one million refugees facing death and starvation.

House of Representatives Republican Leader Dick Armey praised Clinton for consulting with Congress in advance on the possible dispatch of U.S. troops, saying the consultations had "been more encouraging" than in his past dealings with the White House.
But other Republicans were still wary about sending troops.
Oklahoma Republican Don Nickles, the Senate Republican Whip, said on "Fox News Sunday" that he was not opposed to a humanitarian mission, but was not certain it was needed.
"I have reservations as whether we are needed, but if our intervention will save hundreds of thousands of lives I'm for it, but I'm not sure it's needed," he said.
"I'm not sure we help by sending troops. We might help more by giving some financial assistance to the relief agencies," he said.
Robert Oakley, the former U.S. ambassador to Zaire, said a military mission was needed in any event to help refugees in the southern part of Zaire.

He said there were "300,000-400,000 refugees in south Zaire who can't get back because of intimidation and it seems the sort of operation envisaged for the north and south needs to be carried out in the south."
